features.name: Flaky, mostly vacuous test: a non-yielding handler gets recovered
features.description: test/docs-worker-guide/cpu-intensive.test.ts 'a non-yielding handler starves heartbeats and gets recovered' [tcp] failed once in 3 unchanged host runs on 2f1ad824 (2026-11-13, during the test-suite-speedups baseline: 'timed out waiting for the blocked job to be recovered by the broker' after 30 s). The handler busy-loops 3 s in the test process, which also hosts the broker (embedded manager or the in-process TCP server), so no stall sweep can run during the block, and the job then completes. The wait accepts state 'waiting', the job's state before the worker pulls it, so the test passes only when its first poll beats the pull and fails when the pull wins. Make it observe real recovery (for example a broker in another process, or a block that outlasts several sweeps of a short stallCheckMs while the broker's timers can fire) without weakening the page's claim; reproduce the flake first.

features.name: PostgreSQL completion-retention prune: a 10 s nested-loop plan on a fresh namespace
features.description: Found on 2026-11-13 while reproducing postgres-sigkill-hook-timeout-flake (PostgreSQL 17.12). The candidate SELECT of prunePostgresCompletionTombstoneBatch (src/infrastructure/persistence/postgres/completionLifecycle.ts) ran 10,360 ms with 44,050,096 shared-buffer hits on 290 completions, 256 dependencies and 290 jobs of one namespace. That is EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) after the first four tests of test/postgres-public-api-extreme.test.ts, with the tables auto-analyzed. The planner estimated one row for the namespace and chose nested-loop anti joins whose index conditions use only namespace (Join Filter dependency.job_id = consumer.id, 74,240 inner index scans of bunqueue_jobs_pkey). The query runs while it holds the namespace's completion-retention advisory lock. The other brokers' 60 s sweeps wait for it and fail with lock_timeout (seen in CI run 43355036181 and locally), and a broker whose sweep is in flight delays its graceful shutdown. Reproduce first with a deterministic test (the plan, or a duration bound on a fresh namespace), then rewrite the query without changing which tombstones are pruned; measure it before and after.

Host checks before the gate: 2026-11-13, base 2f1ad824, branch postgres-completion-prune-plan, uncommitted (git add -A only). Root cause: the plan, not a missing index. Every check already has a full-key index (bunqueue_jobs_pkey, bunqueue_dependencies_dependency_idx); for a namespace the statistics do not cover (analyzed before the namespace had rows, or other namespaces only) every scan is estimated at 1 row, so the planner keeps unparameterized namespace-only scans inside nested-loop anti joins (Join Filter dependency.job_id = consumer.id) and rescans the namespace's jobs once per completion and per dependency: cubic work under the completion-retention advisory lock. The per-batch DELETE recheck has the same shape and the same failure. Reproduction on disposable postgres:16-alpine (16.16), 17-alpine (17.12) and 18.6-alpine (18.6), macOS host: CI-shaped data (290 completions, 256 dependencies, 290 jobs) 1,626 ms on 17.12 with 74,240 loops of the inner jobs scan; 619 completions, 512 dependencies, 298 jobs: candidate SELECT 10,877 / 10,658 / 10,241 ms (16/17/18) with 74,396,420 shared hits and 276,148 loops, DELETE recheck 10,811 / 10,348 / 11,002 ms. features.name: Worker.close(true) waits a full command timeout after its broker died
features.description: Every CI run of the SIGKILL recovery case of test/postgres-public-api-extreme.test.ts takes about 45.3 s (16 of 16 PostgreSQL jobs sampled on 2026-11-13), and locally victim.close(true) returns 45,101-45,105 ms after its broker was SIGKILLed. A forced close still waits for a best-effort command to the dead broker until the client's commandTimeout (45 s in that harness). It fails no test, but it moves the end of that file into the brokers' first 60 s sweep (see postgres-sigkill-hook-timeout-flake), and a forced close of a Worker whose broker is gone is as slow as the command bound. Measure which close step waits (the release of the active job, the ACK flush or UnregisterWorker), then decide whether a forced close should bound or skip best-effort commands to an unreachable broker; that is a behavior change and needs its own decision.
features.evidence: Not implemented; needs an owner decision: is a bounded forced close allowed to drop the final ACK flush to an unreachable broker? Ship only in a minor or major with an upgrade note. Measured 2026-11-13 on base 2f1ad824 (worker-close-fixes session, code removed from that change-set). Which step waits: UnregisterWorker (probe with commandTimeout 3 s, broker killed: sent at +101 ms, settled after 3,001 ms, close(true) 3,103 ms); buffered-job MoveToWait and an ACK flush queued for a killed broker wait the same way, the flush up to four timeouts. Reproduction (fake broker, commandTimeout 10 s), before: killed broker 10,101 ms, close(true) during a graceful drain 10,103 ms, ACK flush to a killed broker 40,704 ms, connection dropping 1 s into the forced close 41,807 ms, live broker answering ACKB after 7 s 7,097 ms, half-open broker with pings disabled 10,102 ms. Candidate tried (a 5 s grace, FORCE_CLOSE_GRACE_MS, armed only while the Worker's pool has no connected client, checked every 50 ms, then the pool is closed): 5,131 / 5,134 / 5,736 / 6,744 ms, live 7 s ACKB 7,098 ms delivered and confirmed, half-open 10,103 ms; --rerun-each 20 120 / 0. Skeptic round 1 FAIL (an unconditional grace cut a live slow broker); round 2 CONDITIONAL: a broker that restarts and stays down longer than 5 s during close(true) used to receive the queued ACK flush after the reconnect, while the grace cuts it, so completed jobs can run again. Under the release-compatibility rule this is a behavior change, not a defect fix.
